title: Do Students Care About Our Efforts?
author: Daniel Golazeski
summary: Daniel Golazeski recounts a graduation-day thank-you from a former student, Eric, for whom he had made daily video lessons through COVID scheduling chaos and spent more than two hundred hours of after-school help. To his surprise, Eric was not thanking him for any of that. He was thanking him for a few hallway conversations in the year Golazeski did not teach him, which Eric said had helped with his mental health. The teacher reads this as sobering and humbling, since the video work was something only a few colleagues could have done while the conversations were something anyone could do. His conclusion is that students do care about our efforts, but not always the kind that earns an "Exceeds Expectations" on an evaluation. What students often need most is an adult who asks how they are doing, listens and offers encouragement.
points: The effort that mattered most to the student was thirty minutes of hallway conversation across ten months, not two hundred hours of instructional extras.
Relational attention is available to every adult in a school and requires no special certification or content knowledge.
Evaluation systems reward visible instructional effort and are blind to the small contacts students may value most.
A former teacher can still matter in a student's senior year, so check-ins do not need to be limited to the students on your roster.
quotes: I’ve been thanked by students before, but the way Eric phrased his gratitude strapped me into a short, but frantic roller coaster of emotions.
Every day, I created a video of an Honors Algebra 2 lesson that Eric could watch while I taught the rest of the class a regular Algebra 2 lesson.
Between his sophomore and junior years, I spent more than two hundred hours working after school helping Eric learn. But that wasn’t what he wanted to thank me for.
How could thirty minutes of polite conversation spread out over ten months have more of an impact than two hundred hours of my genuine hard work?
Even today, years after I heard these four words, they still hit me like a left hook I never saw coming.
During his senior year, I just talked to him. That’s something anyone could have done. And, to Eric, that effort mattered more.
Sometimes, what students care most about, what students need more than anything, is to have an adult in their lives who asks how they’re doing, listens to them, and offers genuine encouragement.
That doesn’t require any special certification or content knowledge. We can all do that. We should all do that.
